He wrote slowly, thinking aloud. 'Room, fourteen. Food, if I cook some days, seven. Auto, with the room so close, maybe one. Phone, five hundred. Electricity and water, one.' He stopped. 'Twenty-three and a half. Out of thirty.'
'And the shared flat you're in now?'

He sat back. Three thousand a month for a shorter commute. He folded the napkin into his wallet and said he would decide after one more week of the long bus ride.

I'm Trisha, and in March I ran out of money four days before salary for the second month in a row. I'd guessed a budget in January, a neat one, and it clearly wasn't real.
So in April I did something boring. Every time I paid on my phone, I wrote it in a notes file that evening: amount, what, why. My flatmate Sarika laughed at me the first week.

So now there's a cap, ₹1,200 a week for delivery, and Sarika and I cook double on Sundays. In May I reached salary day with ₹2,000 left.

Lakshmi, an analyst in her first year, came in upset. She has been following a 50-30-20 split from a video her friend shared: half for needs, thirty percent for wants, twenty for savings. 'It's the rule everyone uses,' she said.
Her month doesn't fit it. She sends ₹10,000 home to her parents every month, and her share of the flat, with deposit instalments, takes another ₹11,000. On ₹34,000, that alone is more than half. To keep the 'twenty percent savings', she had been skipping meals and borrowing from a flatmate.

'That's, what, a year?'

The city was shut for a bandh on the day Pallavi's first salary arrived, so there was nothing to buy and nowhere to go. She sat on her hostel bed with ₹27,000 on the screen and a notebook on her knees.
Her friends kept sending pictures of new shoes and weekend trips. She wrote her own wants down honestly: shoes, a trip to Goa with the team, a better phone. Then, above all of it, she wrote two lines. Maa and Baba: ₹6,000. Her brother Jagdish's coaching fees: ₹3,000.
She talked it through under her breath. 'If I put those first, I'm choosing them. If I put them last, I'm just hoping something's left.' She looked at the page. 'Jagdish only gets one shot at his boards.'
She sent both amounts before the bandh ended. The trip she crossed out, for now. The shoes stayed, a cheaper pair. It stung a little less than she had expected.

That night, in his rented room in Saidapet, he redid his plan on the back of the bike brochure. At the top he wrote: Amma-Appa, ₹5,000 a month. Aditi's fees: this semester's sent this week, then ₹3,000 a month saved toward each one. Then rent and food. Then, last, 'bike'.

subtype: Approach: planning fallacy about irregular expenses [Pitfall]
passage:
1 September. Disha finishes her first real budget with her flatmate Jomon watching. Every month fits: rent, food, travel, phone, a neat ₹4,000 saving. 'Balanced,' she says, and pins it to the fridge.
14 October. A message from the insurer: the yearly premium on her health policy, ₹6,200, is due in two weeks. Disha stares at the fridge sheet. There is no line for it. She pays it from the savings, which leaves almost nothing there.
2 November. Her laptop won't turn on, the week before Diwali. Repair: ₹4,500. She has also promised gifts for her nieces. Jomon lends her ₹3,000 until salary. That night she adds a new column to the fridge sheet, with the premium, repairs and gifts, and grimaces at how much smaller the monthly saving looks now.

qa.q: How much was the yearly premium?
qa.a: The yearly premium was ₹6,200.

qa.q: How does Disha feel as she adds the new column?
qa.a: Disha is frustrated and a bit embarrassed, grimacing at how small the saving looks once the lumpy costs are counted.

qa.q: What would you change first in Disha's original plan?
qa.a: Add a line for yearly and one-off costs like premiums, repairs and festival gifts from the start, so they are planned rather than surprises.

qa.q: What is it like for Jomon to watch the plan come apart?
qa.a: Jomon saw the neat sheet go up and then has to step in with a loan, which may feel caring but a little worrying too.

grounding: Shows a monthly budget that leaves out a yearly premium, a laptop repair and festival gifts, so two lumpy bills in one quarter break it.

subtype: Approach: planning fallacy about irregular expenses [Pitfall]
passage:
Himani, you showed me your budget sheet. Very neat. Let your Joseph uncle tell you about mine, from my first job at the Kochi port office.
I made a sheet just like yours. Rent, food, bus, the money home to Amma. Everything monthly. I even saved a little every month and felt very clever.
Then, in one quarter, two things came that weren't monthly. In November, the premium for the life policy Appachan had taken out in my name, a full year at once. In December, Christmas: gifts for eleven cousins, and my share of my sister's wedding saree. My clever savings were gone by the 10th of December, and I borrowed from the office cooperative to finish the month.
What I didn't have was a line for the things that come once a year. After that, I always had one. So, Himani, where is that line on your sheet?

qa.q: What came due in November?
qa.a: The premium for the life policy, a full year at once.

qa.q: How did young Joseph feel about the budget before the two bills arrived?
qa.a: Joseph felt clever and confident, saving a little every month, which made the December shock more deflating.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept Joseph from borrowing?
qa.a: Adding a line for yearly costs like the premium and Christmas gifts, and putting a little toward them each month.

qa.q: How might Joseph's sister have felt about the saree share if she had known it meant borrowing?
qa.a: She might have been touched by the gift but uneasy that her brother had to borrow to give it.

grounding: Shows a monthly-only budget broken by a yearly premium and festival costs in the same quarter.
